Negative Appraisals.value: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power
I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

vignette:
Tariq, a 41-year-old married Middle Eastern American, had built a life around the vibrant expression of movement, his body a canvas for stories and emotions as a professional dancer. Yet, for years, an invisible weight had pressed down on him, a legacy of the time he spent as a civilian caught in a war zone during his youth. He remembered vividly the day his village was shelled, the ground trembling underfoot, the acrid smell of dust and burning earth filling the air. He had been trying to help a neighbor, a young boy whose name, Sami, was screamed by his distraught mother amidst the chaos, a sound that echoed in Tariq's mind long after the attack subsided.

Now, decades later, the world around him held countless traps. A car backfiring on the street or the distant, muffled thud of construction work could instantly transport him back, the sound a visceral echo of the shelling. Even the mundane aroma of damp soil after a rainstorm, or the dry, dusty smell of an outdoor market, would flood his senses, pulling him into a terrifying re-experience. And when he heard a name like Sami, or any name similar in cadence, it was as if the past reached out and gripped him anew.

These sudden intrusions, these triggers, had a profound and immediate effect on Tariq's inner world, shaping how he saw himself and others. When the sharp crack of a dropped prop backstage would pierce the quiet of a rehearsal, Tariq would flinch, his heart seizing in his chest. In the immediate aftermath, a profound sense of emotional numbness would wash over him; he had come to believe, in those moments, that he was fundamentally "dead inside," a hollow shell incapable of genuine feeling. This conviction deepened with each jarring reminder of his past. Similarly, the earthy scent of the potted plants in the dance studio lobby could send shivers down his spine, making him feel acutely vulnerable. In those moments, he became certain, with agonizing clarity, that others could see what had happened to him just by looking at him, as if the trauma were etched across his face for all to witness, stripping him bare of any pretense of normalcy.

This pervasive feeling of being exposed and emotionally barren began to corrode his passion. Dancing, once his sanctuary and his voice, became a source of intense anxiety. He found it increasingly difficult to inhabit the characters and convey the nuanced emotions required for his performances, feeling disconnected from his own body and the music. The belief that he was "dead inside" made it hard to access the joy or sorrow his roles demanded, rendering his movements stiff and his expressions vacant. When performing, the thought that others could see what had happened to him just by looking at him was crippling; he would often avoid eye contact with the audience, his gaze fixed on the floor, convinced they were scrutinizing his hidden wounds rather than his art. This led to a noticeable decline in his stage presence and, consequently, fewer principal roles, impacting his professional standing.

His marriage also suffered. His wife, though supportive, struggled to connect with the withdrawn man he had become. Tariq, grappling with the profound sense that he had lost his faith in people, life, or a higher power, found himself unable to trust fully, even those closest to him. He felt isolated in his suffering, believing that no one could truly understand, and this further solidified his conviction that he was fundamentally alone, cut off from the human connection he once cherished. The cumulative effect of these struggles, the increasing distance from his art and his loved ones, finally compelled Tariq to seek help. He arrived at therapy exhausted, hoping to reclaim some semblance of the vibrant man he once was, but deeply afraid that the numbness and exposure were now permanent parts of him.
